responses: Natural Language Processing (NLP) is the field of AI that lets computers read, interpret and generate human language. Typical applications are chatbots, translation, search, sentiment analysis and summarisation.

NLP combines linguistics and machine learning so software can work with text and speech: splitting text into tokens, turning words into numbers, then learning patterns such as intent, sentiment or entities.
In short: NLP turns unstructured human language into structured data that a model can learn from, which powers chatbots, translators, search engines and voice assistants.

responses: I clean each message in stages: lowercase it, strip URLs and punctuation, tokenize it with NLTK, drop a few filler words, and stem the rest with the Snowball stemmer. Then TF-IDF (word n-grams plus character n-grams) turns it into numbers.

Preprocessing = normalisation (lowercase, remove noise) + tokenization + stop-word removal + stemming. After that, TF-IDF weights words by how informative they are, so rare, meaningful terms count more than common ones.
Stemming trims words to a root ('training' → 'train'), stop words are very common words with little meaning, and TF-IDF converts the cleaned tokens into weighted numeric features.

responses: The project is pure Python: NLTK for tokenization and stemming, scikit-learn for TF-IDF features and the Logistic Regression classifier, Flask for the web interface, and joblib to save the trained model.

NLTK handles the language processing, scikit-learn does the machine learning, and Flask serves the chat page. spaCy and TensorFlow are good alternatives: spaCy for fast production pipelines, TensorFlow for neural models such as LSTMs.
Dependencies are listed in requirements.txt: nltk, scikit-learn, numpy, joblib and flask. Install them with pip install -r requirements.txt.

responses: I'm trained with supervised learning: each example sentence in data/intents.json is labelled with an intent, converted to TF-IDF features, and a Logistic Regression classifier learns to map features to intents. Run python train.py to (re)train.
To teach me something new, add example phrases (and responses) to data/intents.json, then run python train.py and python evaluate.py to check that accuracy improved.
Training takes about a second because the model is small: a TF-IDF vectoriser plus a linear classifier, saved to models/intent_model.joblib.

responses: Intent recognition means classifying what the user wants. I predict the most likely intent and a confidence score, then reply with a response written for that intent. If confidence is low, I search my knowledge base, and if nothing matches I ask you to rephrase.
My answers are template-based: every intent has several prewritten replies and I pick one. That's reliable and predictable, but unlike a generative model I can't answer beyond what I was taught.
The confidence threshold decides when I trust a prediction. Below it I try retrieving a passage from data/knowledge_base.txt, and failing that I use a safe fallback instead of guessing.

responses: Run python evaluate.py for cross-validated accuracy, a held-out test on separately written paraphrases, a per-intent precision/recall/F1 report, a confusion matrix and the list of misclassified phrases. The results are saved in reports/.
I improve by reviewing misclassified phrases from evaluate.py, adding varied examples for weak intents, and re-training. Unit tests (python -m unittest discover -s tests) guard against regressions.
I can be wrong: I'm a small model trained on a limited dataset. Accuracy is measured on phrases the model never saw during training, and low-confidence predictions fall back to a safe reply.

responses: The training data is data/intents.json: a hand-written set of labelled example phrases ('patterns') and replies for each intent, collected for this project. data/knowledge_base.txt holds longer passages used for retrieval.
Each intent has a tag, around 30 example phrases and several responses. To extend the bot, add more varied phrases per intent, since variety matters more than volume.
The dataset is small and curated, which is fine for a learning project but is why accuracy depends on how well your wording matches the examples.
